claim: SOX2 is central in establishing and maintaining pluripotency.
source: The transcription factor SOX2 is central in establishing and maintaining pluripotency.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about SOX2's role in pluripotency.

claim: SOX2 is O-GlcNAc modified in its transactivation domain during reprogramming.
source: Here, we show SOX2 is O-GlcNAc modified in its transactivation domain during reprogramming and in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: SOX2 is O-GlcNAc modified in its transactivation domain in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs).
source: Here, we show SOX2 is O-GlcNAc modified in its transactivation domain during reprogramming and in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: SOX2 O-GlcNAcylation at serine 248 is decreased upon induction of differentiation.
source: Upon induction of differentiation SOX2 O-GlcNAcylation at serine 248 is decreased.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing undifferentiated and differentiated cells shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Replacing wild type SOX2 with an O-GlcNAc-deficient SOX2 (S248A) increases reprogramming efficiency.
source: Replacing wild type with an O-GlcNAc-deficient SOX2 (S248A) increases reprogramming efficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from reprogramming experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ESCs with O-GlcNAc-deficient SOX2 exhibit alterations in gene expression.
source: ESCs with O-GlcNAc-deficient SOX2 exhibit alterations in gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: O-GlcNAc-deficient SOX2 exhibits altered protein-protein interactions compared to wild type.
source: This change correlates with altered protein-protein interactions and genomic occupancy of the O-GlcNAc-deficient SOX2 compared to wild type.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data presented in Figure 6.

claim: O-GlcNAc-deficient SOX2 exhibits altered genomic occupancy compared to wild type.
source: This change correlates with altered protein-protein interactions and genomic occupancy of the O-GlcNAc-deficient SOX2 compared to wild type.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data presented in Figure 5.

claim: SOX2 O-GlcNAcylation impairs the SOX2-PARP1 interaction.
source: In addition, SOX2 O-GlcNAcylation impairs the SOX2-PARP1 interaction, which has been shown to regulate ESC self-renewal.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro pulldown experiments shown in Figure 6D and by citation to previous work on PARP1's role in ESC self-renewal.

claim: The SOX2-PARP1 interaction has been shown to regulate ESC self-renewal.
source: In addition, SOX2 O-GlcNAcylation impairs the SOX2-PARP1 interaction, which has been shown to regulate ESC self-renewal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SOX2 is necessary for embryonic stem cell (ESC) self-renewal.
source: SOX2 (sex determining region Y-box 2) is a transcription factor necessary for embryonic stem cell (ESC) self-renewal (Arnold et al., 2011; Masui et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Increased expression of SOX2 interferes with self-renewal and pluripotency.
source: Precise control of SOX2 is critical for ESC maintenance, since increased or decreased expression of SOX2 interferes with self-renewal and pluripotency (Kopp et al., 2008; Masui et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Decreased expression of SOX2 interferes with self-renewal and pluripotency.
source: Precise control of SOX2 is critical for ESC maintenance, since increased or decreased expression of SOX2 interferes with self-renewal and pluripotency (Kopp et al., 2008; Masui et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SOX2 is reported to be phosphorylated.
source: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) of SOX2 may play a role in its regulation, as SOX2 is reported to be phosphorylated, methylated, ubiquitinylated, SUMOylated, acetylated, and PARylated (Baltus et al., 2009; Brumbaugh et al., 2012; Fang et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2009; Lai et al., 2012; Swaney et al., 2009; Tahmasebi et al., 2013; Tsuruzoe et al., 2006; Van Hoof et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SOX2 is reported to be methylated.
source: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) of SOX2 may play a role in its regulation, as SOX2 is reported to be phosphorylated, methylated, ubiquitinylated, SUMOylated, acetylated, and PARylated (Baltus et al., 2009; Brumbaugh et al., 2012; Fang et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2009; Lai et al., 2012; Swaney et al., 2009; Tahmasebi et al., 2013; Tsuruzoe et al., 2006; Van Hoof et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SOX2 is reported to be ubiquitinylated.
source: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) of SOX2 may play a role in its regulation, as SOX2 is reported to be phosphorylated, methylated, ubiquitinylated, SUMOylated, acetylated, and PARylated (Baltus et al., 2009; Brumbaugh et al., 2012; Fang et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2009; Lai et al., 2012; Swaney et al., 2009; Tahmasebi et al., 2013; Tsuruzoe et al., 2006; Van Hoof et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SOX2 is reported to be SUMOylated.
source: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) of SOX2 may play a role in its regulation, as SOX2 is reported to be phosphorylated, methylated, ubiquitinylated, SUMOylated, acetylated, and PARylated (Baltus et al., 2009; Brumbaugh et al., 2012; Fang et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2009; Lai et al., 2012; Swaney et al., 2009; Tahmasebi et al., 2013; Tsuruzoe et al., 2006; Van Hoof et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SOX2 is reported to be acetylated.
source: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) of SOX2 may play a role in its regulation, as SOX2 is reported to be phosphorylated, methylated, ubiquitinylated, SUMOylated, acetylated, and PARylated (Baltus et al., 2009; Brumbaugh et al., 2012; Fang et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2009; Lai et al., 2012; Swaney et al., 2009; Tahmasebi et al., 2013; Tsuruzoe et al., 2006; Van Hoof et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SOX2 is reported to be PARylated.
source: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) of SOX2 may play a role in its regulation, as SOX2 is reported to be phosphorylated, methylated, ubiquitinylated, SUMOylated, acetylated, and PARylated (Baltus et al., 2009; Brumbaugh et al., 2012; Fang et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2009; Lai et al., 2012; Swaney et al., 2009; Tahmasebi et al., 2013; Tsuruzoe et al., 2006; Van Hoof et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SOX2 is O-GlcNAc modified in mouse ESCs.
source: We have previously shown SOX2 is O-linked N-acetlyglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modified in mouse ESCs (mESCs) (Myers et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation is the dynamic and regulatory mono-glycosylation of nucleocytosolic proteins catalyzed by a single O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT).
source: O-GlcNAcylation is the dynamic and regulatory mono-glycosylation of nucleocytosolic proteins catalyzed by a single O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and removed by a single hydrolase (OGA/MGEA5/NCOAT).
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about O-GlcNAcylation.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation is removed by a single hydrolase (OGA/MGEA5/NCOAT).
source: O-GlcNAcylation is the dynamic and regulatory mono-glycosylation of nucleocytosolic proteins catalyzed by a single O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and removed by a single hydrolase (OGA/MGEA5/NCOAT).
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about O-GlcNAcylation.

claim: O-GlcNAc signaling is essential for embryo viability.
source: O-GlcNAc signaling is essential for embryo viability (O'Donnell et al., 2004; Shafi et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2012) and mESC self-renewal (Jang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: O-GlcNAc signaling is essential for mESC self-renewal.
source: O-GlcNAc signaling is essential for embryo viability (O'Donnell et al., 2004; Shafi et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2012) and mESC self-renewal (Jang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: OGT is critical for mESC maintenance.
source: While OGT is critical for mESC maintenance, the protein- and site-specific functions of O-GlcNAcylation in mESCs have not been fully elucidated.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge and is supported by the context of previous citations.

claim: LC-MS/MS analysis of SOX2 in self-renewal conditions revealed four main populations of the TAD peptide containing serine 248: unmodified, O-GlcNAcylated at one of two sites (S248 or T258), phosphorylated at S253, and doubly modified with O-GlcNAcylation at S248 and phosphorylation at S253.
source: Liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometric (LC-MS/MS) analysis of SOX2 in self-renewal conditions revealed four main populations of the TAD peptide containing serine 248 (hereinafter referred to as TAD peptide): unmodified, O-GlcNAcylated at one of two sites (S248 or T258), phosphorylated at S253, and doubly modified with O-GlcNAcylation at S248 and phosphorylation at S253, (Figure 1A—figure supplements 1–5).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1A and figure supplements 1-5.

claim: Removal of LIF and addition of RA for 48 hr resulted in a marked decrease in the O-GlcNAc occupancy of the TAD peptide.
source: Removal of LIF and addition of RA for 48 hr resulted in a marked decrease in the O-GlcNAc occupancy of the TAD peptide with no change in the phosphorylation stoichiometry (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by extracted ion chromatograph data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Removal of LIF and addition of RA for 48 hr resulted in no change in the phosphorylation stoichiometry of the TAD peptide.
source: Removal of LIF and addition of RA for 48 hr resulted in a marked decrease in the O-GlcNAc occupancy of the TAD peptide with no change in the phosphorylation stoichiometry (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by extracted ion chromatograph data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of SOX2 S248 is responsive to differentiation cues.
source: These data indicate O-GlcNAcylation of SOX2 S248 is responsive to differentiation cues.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing decreased O-GlcNAcylation upon differentiation.

claim: LC-MS/MS analysis of purified SOX2 six days after transduction of mouse embryonic fibroblasts showed S248 is O-GlcNAcylated.
source: LC-MS/MS analysis of purified SOX2 six days after transduction of mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) showed S248 is O-GlcNAcylated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mutation of S248 to alanine (S248A) resulted in loss of O-GlcNAcylation without affecting the other PTMs of the TAD peptide.
source: In addition, mutation of S248 to alanine (S248A) resulted in loss of O-GlcNAcylation without affecting the other PTMs of the TAD peptide (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by extracted ion chromatograph data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: S248 is O-GlcNAc modified during somatic cell reprogramming.
source: These results demonstrate S248 is O-GlcNAc modified during somatic cell reprogramming and suggest a connection between this SOX2 PTM and pluripotency.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from reprogramming experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is a connection between SOX2 S248 O-GlcNAcylation and pluripotency.
source: These results demonstrate S248 is O-GlcNAc modified during somatic cell reprogramming and suggest a connection between this SOX2 PTM and pluripotency.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation of O-GlcNAcylation during reprogramming.

claim: Nanog-Gfp MEFs transduced with OSS248AKM produced significantly more GFP+ iPSC colonies compared to OSWTKM.
source: Nanog-Gfp MEFs transduced with OSS248AKM produced significantly more GFP+ iPSC colonies compared to OSWTKM (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony counting data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: iPSCs generated with OSS248AKM exhibited standard colony morphology.
source: iPSCs generated with OSS248AKM exhibited standard colony morphology and contributed to chimeric mice capable of germ line transmission (Figure 2E), indicating these OSS248AKM iPSCs exhibit the features of normal iPSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by visual observation shown in Figure 2E.

claim: iPSCs generated with OSS248AKM contributed to chimeric mice capable of germ line transmission.
source: iPSCs generated with OSS248AKM exhibited standard colony morphology and contributed to chimeric mice capable of germ line transmission (Figure 2E), indicating these OSS248AKM iPSCs exhibit the features of normal iPSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by chimera data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: OSS248AKM iPSCs exhibit the features of normal iPSCs.
source: iPSCs generated with OSS248AKM exhibited standard colony morphology and contributed to chimeric mice capable of germ line transmission (Figure 2E), indicating these OSS248AKM iPSCs exhibit the features of normal iPSCs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the morphology and chimera data.

claim: Western blot and immunostaining of MEFs transduced with OSFLAG-WTKM or OSFLAG-S248AKM showed equal levels of exogenous SOX2 for the first six days of reprogramming.
source: By Western blot and immunostaining of MEFs transduced with OSFLAG-WTKM or OSFLAG-S248AKM showed equal levels of exogenous SOX2 for the first six days ofof reprogramming (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating comparable expression of WT and S248A triple FLAG tagged SOX2.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: OGT levels were similar for the first six days of reprogramming between OSFLAG-WTKM and OSFLAG-S248AKM transduced MEFs.
source: OGT levels were also similar for the first six days of reprogramming between OSFLAG-WTKM and OSFLAG-S248AKM transduced MEFs (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: SOX2S248A is more efficient than wild type SOX2 at inducing pluripotency.
source: These results indicate that SOX2S248A is more efficient than wild type SOX2 at inducing pluripotency and suggest O-GlcNAcylation at S248 inhibits SOX2 activity.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the reprogramming efficiency data.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation at S248 inhibits SOX2 activity.
source: These results indicate that SOX2S248A is more efficient than wild type SOX2 at inducing pluripotency and suggest O-GlcNAcylation at S248 inhibits SOX2 activity.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the increased reprogramming efficiency of the S248A mutant.

claim: The homologous SOX2 residue has been reported to be phosphorylated in human ESCs.
source: The homologous SOX2 residue has been reported to be phosphorylated in human ESCs (Swaney et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The S248D mutation increased reprogramming efficiency.
source: Therefore, we performed reprogramming experiments using the phospho-mimetic SOX2 mutant, S248D. This mutation also increased reprogramming efficiency (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting it is the removal of an O-GlcNAcylation site, and not of a phosphorylation site, which mediates the effect on SOX2 activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by reprogramming data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: It is the removal of an O-GlcNAcylation site, and not of a phosphorylation site, which mediates the effect on SOX2 activity.
source: Therefore, we performed reprogramming experiments using the phospho-mimetic SOX2 mutant, S248D. This mutation also increased reprogramming efficiency (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting it is the removal of an O-GlcNAcylation site, and not of a phosphorylation site, which mediates the effect on SOX2 activity.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that both S248A and S248D mutations increase reprogramming efficiency.

claim: SOX2 levels in fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg mESCs are comparable to SOX2 levels in the 2TS22C parental cell line.
source: SOX2 levels in fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg mESCs are comparable to SOX2 levels in the 2TS22C parental cell line and nucleo-cytoplasmic distribution was not altered by the mutation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Nucleo-cytoplasmic distribution of SOX2 was not altered by the S248A mutation.
source: SOX2 levels in fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg mESCs are comparable to SOX2 levels in the 2TS22C parental cell line and nucleo-cytoplasmic distribution was not altered by the mutation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: OCT4 and NANOG abundance and distribution were comparable between fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg mESCs.
source: OCT4 and NANOG abundance and distribution were comparable between fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg mESCs (Figure 3C), arguing that there is no gross effect on these pluripotency transcription factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is no gross effect of the S248A mutation on OCT4 and NANOG pluripotency transcription factors.
source: OCT4 and NANOG abundance and distribution were comparable between fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg mESCs (Figure 3C), arguing that there is no gross effect on these pluripotency transcription factors.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the comparable OCT4 and NANOG levels.

claim: LC-MS/MS analysis of immunopurified SOX2 from fSOX2-Tg mESCs identified nine PTM forms of the SOX2 TAD peptide.
source: LC-MS/MS analysis of immunopurified SOX2 from fSOX2-Tg mESCs identified nine PTM forms of the SOX2 TAD peptide (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In fSOX2-Tg mESCs, unmodified and singly O-GlcNAcylated were the most abundant forms of the SOX2 TAD peptide (33.2 and 44.1% of total TAD, respectively).
source: LC-MS analysis of the TAD peptide precursor masses from fSOX2-Tg mESCs showed unmodified and singly O-GlcNAcylated were the most abundant forms of the SOX2 TAD peptide (33.2 and 44.1% of total TAD, respectively) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by extracted ion chromatograph data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: LC-MS analysis confirmed the loss of S248 O-GlcNAcylation in fS248A-Tg mESCs.
source: LC-MS analysis confirmed the loss of S248 O-GlcNAcylation in fS248A-Tg mESCs (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by extracted ion chromatograph data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The TAD peptide in fS248A-Tg mESCs showed increased phosphorylation at S253, from 10.9 to 18.7% of total TAD.
source: In addition, the TAD peptide in fS248A-Tg mESCs showed increased phosphorylation at S253, from 10.9 to 18.7% of total TAD, suggesting cross talk between phosphorylation and O-GlcNAcylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data.

claim: There is cross talk between phosphorylation and O-GlcNAcylation in the SOX2 TAD peptide.
source: In addition, the TAD peptide in fS248A-Tg mESCs showed increased phosphorylation at S253, from 10.9 to 18.7% of total TAD, suggesting cross talk between phosphorylation and O-GlcNAcylation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the increased phosphorylation observed in the S248A mutant.

claim: 320 genes were up regulated in fS248A-Tg cells compared to fSOX2-Tg cells.
source: Significant changes in mRNA levels were observed, with 320 genes up regulated and 344 genes down regulated in fS248A-Tg cells (Figure 4A) and gene set enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes did not show significant enrichment of any pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 344 genes were down regulated in fS248A-Tg cells compared to fSOX2-Tg cells.
source: Significant changes in mRNA levels were observed, with 320 genes up regulated and 344 genes down regulated in fS248A-Tg cells (Figure 4A) and gene set enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes did not show significant enrichment of any pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes did not show significant enrichment of any pathways.
source: Significant changes in mRNA levels were observed, with 320 genes up regulated and 344 genes down regulated in fS248A-Tg cells (Figure 4A) and gene set enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes did not show significant enrichment of any pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis of the microarray data.

claim: Several genes that promote pluripotency and self-renewal were upregulated in fS248A-Tg cells compared to fSOX2-Tg cells.
source: Several genes that promote pluripotency and self-renewal were upregulated, while several genes associated with differentiation were down-regulated in fS248A-Tg cells compared to WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Several genes associated with differentiation were down-regulated in fS248A-Tg cells compared to fSOX2-Tg cells.
source: Several genes that promote pluripotency and self-renewal were upregulated, while several genes associated with differentiation were down-regulated in fS248A-Tg cells compared to WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The S248A mutation alters the balance between self-renewal and differentiation gene expression in mESCs.
source: These data suggest the S248A mutation alters the balance between self-renewal and differentiation gene expression in mESCs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the differential gene expression data.

claim: fS248A-Tg mESCs were relatively unaffected by OCT4 depletion compared to fSOX2-Tg mESCs.
source: While fSOX2-Tg mESCs exhibited altered cell and colony morphology (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), decreased AP staining (Figure 4D), and decreased expression of Nanog (Figure 4E), fS248A-Tg mESCs were relatively unaffected by OCT4 depletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by AP staining and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: fS248A-Tg mESCs can maintain key features of pluripotency when OCT4 levels are reduced.
source: These data indicate that fS248A-Tg mESCs can maintain key features of pluripotency when OCT4 levels are reduced, and are consistent with a role for the O-GlcNAc modification inhibiting SOX2 activity.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the OCT4 depletion experiments.

claim: The O-GlcNAc modification inhibits SOX2 activity.
source: These data indicate that fS248A-Tg mESCs can maintain key features of pluripotency when OCT4 levels are reduced, and are consistent with a role for the O-GlcNAc modification inhibiting SOX2 activity.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that S248A mutant cells maintain pluripotency better than wild type upon OCT4 depletion.

claim: SOX2 distribution exhibited considerable overlap between fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg mESCs, with 4,191 sites bound in both lines.
source: SOX2 distribution exhibited considerable overlap, with 4,191 sites bound in both lines (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The mutant form of SOX2 occupied 1000 sites not bound by the wild type form.
source: The mutant form of SOX2 occupied 1000 sites not bound by the wild type form (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: De novo motif analysis identified the SOX2 binding motif in fS248A-Tg specific peaks.
source: De novo motif analysis identified the SOX2 binding motif in fS248A-Tg specific peaks (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In mESCs, SOX2 and OCT4 heterodimerize and co-occupy a substantial portion of their target regulatory sequences.
source: In mESCs, SOX2 and OCT4 heterodimerize and co-occupy a substantial portion of their target regulatory sequences (Boyer et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: De novo motif analysis of SOX2 peaks shared between fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg mESCs identified the OCT4:SOX2 motif.
source: De novo motif analysis of SOX2 peaks shared between fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg mESCs identified the OCT4:SOX2 motif (Figure 5D), which was present in 2335 of the shared peaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The OCT4:SOX2 motif was present in 2335 of the shared peaks between fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg mESCs.
source: De novo motif analysis of SOX2 peaks shared between fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg mESCs identified the OCT4:SOX2 motif (Figure 5D), which was present in 2335 of the shared peaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis data.

claim: The OCT4:SOX2 motif was not identified in any of the fS248A-Tg-specific peaks.
source: The OCT4:SOX2 motif was not identified in any of the fS248A-Tg-specific peaks (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The S248A mutation alters SOX2 genomic distribution, increasing its ability to associate with SOX2 binding sites that would not ordinarily be bound by wild type SOX2 in mESCs.
source: These data indicate the S248A mutation alters SOX2 genomic distribution, increasing its ability to associate with SOX2 binding sites that would not ordinarily be bound by wild type SOX2 in mESCs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the ChIP-seq and motif analysis data.

claim: S248 lies in the TAD of SOX2, a region responsible for interactions with transcriptional regulatory machinery.
source: S248 lies in the TAD of SOX2, a region responsible for interactions with transcriptional regulatory machinery (Ambrosetti et al., 2000; Nowling et al., 2000; Yuan et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 329 proteins were enriched in both fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg, but not haSOX2-Tg FLAG IPs.
source: We identified 329 proteins enriched in both fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg, but not haSOX2-Tg FLAG IPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data from co-IP experiments.

claim: Many SOX2 interactors exist in complexes involved in histone modification, DNA damage repair, or nucleosome remodeling.
source: Many of these interactors exist in complexes involved in histone modification, DNA damage repair, or nucleosome remodeling (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the identity of the interacting proteins and their known functions.

claim: fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg cells recapitulate some known SOX2 interactions.
source: Several SOX2 interactors have been previously described (Cox et al., 2013; Engelen et al., 2011; Gao et al., 2012), indicating fSOX2-Tg and fS248A-Tg cells recapitulate some known SOX2 interactions (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the identified interactors with previously published data.

claim: 22 of the interacting proteins were enriched at least four-fold in the co-IP with fSOX2-Tg (z-score > 1.5).
source: 22 of the interacting proteins were enriched at least four-fold in the co-IP with fSOX2-Tg (z-score > 1.5) and 60 were enriched in the fS248A-Tg co-IP (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data from co-IP experiments.

claim: 60 of the interacting proteins were enriched in the fS248A-Tg co-IP.
source: 22 of the interacting proteins were enriched at least four-fold in the co-IP with fSOX2-Tg (z-score > 1.5) and 60 were enriched in the fS248A-Tg co-IP (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data from co-IP experiments.

claim: Co-IP followed by Western blotting showed preferential enrichment of PARP1 with mutant SOX2.
source: Co-IP followed by Western blotting corroborated the IP-MS data, showing preferential enrichment of PARP1 and GATAD2B with mutant and wild type SOX2, respectively, while SMARCA4 was associated equally with both forms of SOX2 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Co-IP followed by Western blotting showed preferential enrichment of GATAD2B with wild type SOX2.
source: Co-IP followed by Western blotting corroborated the IP-MS data, showing preferential enrichment of PARP1 and GATAD2B with mutant and wild type SOX2, respectively, while SMARCA4 was associated equally with both forms of SOX2 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: SMARCA4 was associated equally with both wild type and mutant forms of SOX2.
source: Co-IP followed by Western blotting corroborated the IP-MS data, showing preferential enrichment of PARP1 and GATAD2B with mutant and wild type SOX2, respectively, while SMARCA4 was associated equally with both forms of SOX2 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: MBD3 and MTA3 were consistently enriched in fS248A-Tg co-IPs while other NuRD components were enriched with fSOX2-Tg.
source: For example, MBD3 and MTA3, both of which can be a part of the NuRD complex, were consistently enriched in fS248A-Tg co-IPs while other NuRD components were enriched with fSOX2-Tg (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by targeted proteomic analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Targeted analysis showed the majority of the NuRD complex preferentially associated with SOX2WT, while MBD3 and MTA3 components prefer SOX2S248A.
source: Targeted analysis showed the majority of the NuRD complex preferentially associated with SOX2WT, while MBD3 and MTA3 components prefer SOX2S248A (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by targeted proteomic analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The S248A mutation can affect the stoichiometry of subunits in complexes that associate with SOX2.
source: These results suggest that the S248A mutation can affect the stoichiometry of subunits in complexes that associate with SOX2.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the differential association of NuRD subunits with wild type and mutant SOX2.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of Bio-SOX2 by recombinant human OGT depended on the sugar donor UDP-GlcNAc.
source: O-GlcNAcylation of Bio-tagged, recombinant human SOX2 (Bio-SOX2, 96% identical to mouse) by recombinant human OGT (His-OGT, 99% identical to mouse), which depended on the sugar donor UDP-GlcNAc, was detected by Western blotting (Figure 6D) and specificity confirmed by mass spec (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pull down efficiency of Bio-SOX2 was not affected by O-GlcNAcylation.
source: Pull down efficiency of Bio-SOX2 was not affected by O-GlcNAcylation and His-OGT was not detected in pull downs, indicating any potential SOX2:OGT interaction was not stable under our wash conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data from the pulldown experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: His-OGT was not detected in pull downs, indicating any potential SOX2:OGT interaction was not stable under the wash conditions.
source: Pull down efficiency of Bio-SOX2 was not affected by O-GlcNAcylation and His-OGT was not detected in pull downs, indicating any potential SOX2:OGT interaction was not stable under our wash conditions.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the absence of His-OGT in the pulldown.

claim: Unmodified Bio-SOX2 pulled down GST-PARP1, indicating the interaction between mouse SOX2 and PARP1 can be recapitulated by their conserved human homologues.
source: Unmodified Bio-SOX2 pulled down GST-PARP1, indicating the interaction between mouse SOX2 and PARP1 can be recapitulated by their conserved human homologues.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data from the pulldown experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Pulldown efficiency of GST-PARP1 by glycosylated Bio-SOX2 was diminished compared to that of unmodified Bio-SOX2.
source: Pulldown efficiency of GST-PARP1 by glycosylated Bio-SOX2 was diminished compared to that of unmodified Bio-SOX2 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data from the pulldown experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: SOX2 O-GlcNAcylation directly alters its interaction with a transcriptional regulatory protein involved in maintaining the balance of self-renewal and differentiation.
source: Together, these data demonstrate SOX2 O-GlcNAcylation directly alters its interaction with a transcriptional regulatory protein involved in maintaining the balance of self-renewal and differentiation (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the in vitro pulldown data and the known role of PARP1.

claim: Depletion of OGT disrupts mESC self-renewal.
source: Depletion of OGT, the sole enzyme that mediates intracellular O-GlcNAcylation, disrupts mESC self-renewal (O'Donnell et al., 2004; Shafi et al., 2000), prompting us to identify OGT targets to elucidate link between O-GlcNAc and self-renewal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Using an unbiased strategy for enrichment of native O-GlcNAcylated nuclear peptides, SOX2 S248 was identified as an OGT substrate.
source: Using an unbiased strategy for enrichment of native O-GlcNAcylated nuclear peptides, we previously identified SOX2 S248 as an OGT substrate (Myers et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: S248 is O-GlcNAcylated during somatic cell reprogramming.
source: Here, we find that S248 is O-GlcNAcylated during somatic cell reprogramming and that mutation of this residue to alanine increases reprogramming efficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from reprogramming experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mutation of S248 to alanine increases reprogramming efficiency.
source: Here, we find that S248 is O-GlcNAcylated during somatic cell reprogramming and that mutation of this residue to alanine increases reprogramming efficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by reprogramming data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: mESCs expressing SOX2S248A exhibit changes in transcription consistent with increased expression of pluripotency promoting genes at the expense of differentiation promoting genes.
source: We also find mESCs expressing SOX2S248A exhibit changes in transcription consistent with increased expression of pluripotency promoting genes at the expense of differentiation promoting genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The S248A mutation promotes SOX2 activity.
source: Together, these analyses from both mESCs and during somatic cell reprogramming reveal the S248A mutation promotes SOX2 activity, which suggests SOX2 O-GlcNAcylation is inhibitory during maintenance and establishment of pluripotency.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the reprogramming and gene expression data.

claim: SOX2 O-GlcNAcylation is inhibitory during maintenance and establishment of pluripotency.
source: Together, these analyses from both mESCs and during somatic cell reprogramming reveal the S248A mutation promotes SOX2 activity, which suggests SOX2 O-GlcNAcylation is inhibitory during maintenance and establishment of pluripotency.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that removing O-GlcNAcylation increases SOX2 activity.

claim: S248 O-GlcNAcylation is regulated by developmental signaling molecules.
source: Our data indicate that S248 O-GlcNAcylation is regulated by developmental signaling molecules, since removing LIF and adding RA to trigger differentiation resulted in a substantial decrease in this PTM.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the differentiation experiments shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: The decrease in S248 O-GlcNAcylation upon differentiation appears contradictory to the finding that the S248A mutation promotes mESC self-renewal.
source: This decrease in S248 O-GlcNAcylation appears contradictory to the finding that the S248A mutation, which eliminates O-GlcNAcylation, promotes mESC self-renewal.
evidence: This claim is an observation about the apparent contradiction in the data.

claim: The effects of PTMs are likely to be context specific, and determined by the transcription factors and signaling molecules present in each cell type.
source: However, the effects of this, or any, PTM are likely to be context specific, and determined by the transcription factors and signaling molecules present in each cell type.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about PTM function.

claim: GlcNAc-S248 may inhibit SOX2 activity in mESCs.
source: GlcNAc-S248 may inhibit SOX2 activity in mESCs, where the decrease in this PTM may alter SOX2 activity upon differentiation, such that SOX2 functions appropriately for the changing cellular context.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the role of O-GlcNAcylation.

claim: The S248A mutation allows SOX2S248A to occupy sites that SOX2WT is unable to access in mESCs.
source: The majority of these sites contained a predicted SOX2 binding motif, indicating the mutation allows SOX2S248A to occupy sites that SOX2WT is unable to access in mESCs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the ChIP-seq and motif analysis data shown in Figure 5.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation can regulate the affinity of SOX2 for its target sites.
source: This result suggests O-GlcNAcylation can regulate the affinity of SOX2 for its target sites.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the altered genomic occupancy of the S248A mutant.

claim: The mutation or loss of O-GlcNAcylation could affect secondary protein structure and/or PPIs.
source: Since the mutation lies in the TAD, but affects the activity of the high mobility group DNA binding region, the mutation or loss of O-GlcNAcylation could affect secondary protein structure and/or PPIs.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of the mutation's effect.

claim: Single molecule imaging of SOX2 with a deleted TAD showed altered DNA occupancy and higher site-specific residence time.
source: Single molecule imaging of SOX2 with a deleted TAD showed altered DNA occupancy and higher site-specific residence time, supporting the idea that TAD mutations affect SOX2 DNA binding (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Upon OCT4 knockdown, fS248A-Tg mESCs did not exhibit as dramatic a change in colony morphology as fSOX2-Tg mESCs.
source: Upon OCT4 knockdown, fS248A-Tg mESCs did not exhibit as dramatic a change in colony morphology as fSOX2-Tg mESCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by AP staining data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The new sites of genomic occupancy seen in fS248A-Tg mESCs did not have nearby predicted OCT4 motifs.
source: In addition, the new sites of genomic occupancy seen in fS248A-Tg mESCs did not have nearby predicted OCT4 motifs.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The O-GlcNAc-deficient SOX2 may exhibit an altered reliance on OCT4 for binding and regulation of gene expression.
source: Together these results suggest the O-GlcNAc-deficient SOX2 may exhibit an altered reliance on OCT4 for binding and regulation of gene expression.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the OCT4 knockdown and ChIP-seq data.

claim: Many of the proteins that exhibited differential interaction between wild type and mutant SOX2 are components of complexes implicated in chromatin regulation.
source: Many of the proteins that exhibited differential interaction between wild type and mutant SOX2 are components of complexes implicated in chromatin regulation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the identity of the differentially interacting proteins.

claim: The altered associations between SOX2 and chromatin regulatory complexes may underlie the transcriptional and genomic occupancy changes seen in the mutant mESCs.
source: These altered associations may underlie the transcriptional and genomic occupancy changes seen in the mutant mESCs.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the mechanism underlying the observed changes.

claim: Components of the PARP-XRCC and the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) complexes were enriched with SOX2S248A.
source: In addition, components of the PARP-XRCC and the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) complexes were enriched with SOX2S248A, suggesting the possibility that these complexes may function in transcriptional regulation in addition to DNA repair.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data from co-IP experiments.

claim: PARP-XRCC and DNA mismatch repair complexes may function in transcriptional regulation in addition to DNA repair.
source: In addition, components of the PARP-XRCC and the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) complexes were enriched with SOX2S248A, suggesting the possibility that these complexes may function in transcriptional regulation in addition to DNA repair.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the enrichment of these complexes with SOX2.

claim: DNA damage complexes promote mESC self-renewal and iPSC generation.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, DNA damage complexes promote mESC self-renewal and iPSC generation (Fong et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PARP1 interaction with SOX2 is disrupted by O-GlcNAc.
source: We found PARP1 interaction with SOX2 is disrupted by O-GlcNAc and decreased GlcNAc-S248 in differentiating ESCs, consistent with a model in which the developmentally regulated decrease in S248 O-GlcNAcylation promotes PARP1 interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro pulldown data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Decreased GlcNAc-S248 in differentiating ESCs is consistent with a model in which the developmentally regulated decrease in S248 O-GlcNAcylation promotes PARP1 interaction.
source: We found PARP1 interaction with SOX2 is disrupted by O-GlcNAc and decreased GlcNAc-S248 in differentiating ESCs, consistent with a model in which the developmentally regulated decrease in S248 O-GlcNAcylation promotes PARP1 interaction.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the differentiation and pulldown data.

claim: During differentiation, the SOX2-PARP1 interaction inhibits SOX2 binding to enhancers of genes that are necessary for self-renewal.
source: During differentiation, the SOX2-PARP1 interaction inhibits SOX2 binding to enhancers of genes that are necessary for self-renewal (Lai et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SOX2S248A exhibits increased association with PARP1 without decreased occupancy of pluripotency genes under self-renewal conditions.
source: We find that SOX2S248A exhibits increased association with PARP1 without decreased occupancy of pluripotency genes under self-renewal conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP and ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The SOX2-PARP1 interaction alone does not inhibit SOX2 binding to pluripotency gene targets.
source: This result indicates the SOX2-PARP1 interaction alone does not inhibit SOX2 binding to pluripotency gene targets and suggests additional developmentally regulated alterations in SOX2 PTMs or interaction partners contribute to control of SOX2 occupancy.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that increased PARP1 interaction does not decrease pluripotency gene occupancy.

claim: Additional developmentally regulated alterations in SOX2 PTMs or interaction partners contribute to control of SOX2 occupancy.
source: This result indicates the SOX2-PARP1 interaction alone does not inhibit SOX2 binding to pluripotency gene targets and suggests additional developmentally regulated alterations in SOX2 PTMs or interaction partners contribute to control of SOX2 occupancy.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the regulation of SOX2 occupancy.

claim: The increase in SOX2 S253 phosphorylation in fS248A-Tg mESCs suggests there is potential for crosstalk between O-GlcNAcylation and phosphorylation in the TAD peptide in mESCs.
source: The increase in SOX2 S253 phosphorylation in fS248A-Tg mESCs suggests there is potential for crosstalk between O-GlcNAcylation and phosphorylation in the TAD peptide in mESCs.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the increased phosphorylation observed in the S248A mutant.

claim: In general, phosphorylation and O-GlcNAcylation both occur in structurally flexible regions of proteins.
source: In general, phosphorylation and O-GlcNAcylation both occur in structurally flexible regions of proteins, although there is no correlation or anti-correlation in the linear proximity of one PTM to another (Trinidad et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: There is no correlation or anti-correlation in the linear proximity of phosphorylation and O-GlcNAcylation.
source: In general, phosphorylation and O-GlcNAcylation both occur in structurally flexible regions of proteins, although there is no correlation or anti-correlation in the linear proximity of one PTM to another (Trinidad et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: S253 phosphorylation is dispensable for mESC self-renewal.
source: It is unlikely phospho-S253 has a substantial impact on pluripotency gene expression, as S253 phosphorylation is dispensable for mESC self-renewal (Ouyang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The TAD of SOX2 is an unstructured domain.
source: However, because the TAD of SOX2 is an unstructured domain (Reményi et al., 2003), and is O-GlcNAcylated and phosphorylated, the molecular basis for the potential crosstalk may be specific to a different cellular context.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: O-GlcNAc signaling is essential for pluripotency.
source: O-GlcNAc signaling is essential for pluripotency.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge and is supported by previous citations in the manuscript.

claim: Although global O-GlcNAcylation is necessary for mESC self-renewal, a key pillar of pluripotency can be inhibited by O-GlcNAc modification.
source: This study shows that although global O-GlcNAcylation is necessary for mESC self-renewal, a key pillar of pluripotency can be inhibited by O-GlcNAc modification.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the finding that O-GlcNAcylation of SOX2 inhibits its activity while global O-GlcNAcylation is necessary for self-renewal.

claim: This work provides a new mechanism for the regulation of SOX2 through O-GlcNAcylation.
source: This work provides a new mechanism for the regulation of SOX2 through O-GlcNAcylation, and illustrates the role of this PTM in pluripotency and self-renewal is more complex than previously appreciated.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the novel findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The role of O-GlcNAcylation in pluripotency and self-renewal is more complex than previously appreciated.
source: This work provides a new mechanism for the regulation of SOX2 through O-GlcNAcylation, and illustrates the role of this PTM in pluripotency and self-renewal is more complex than previously appreciated.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the findings that O-GlcNAcylation can have both positive (global) and negative (SOX2-specific) effects on pluripotency.
